title: Who Pays a Price on Carbon?
research_question: How are the costs of placing a price on carbon dioxide emissions distributed across households in different income groups in the United States, and to what extent does such a policy impose a disproportionate burden on lower-income households relative to higher-income households? How does the degree of distributional inequity vary with the breadth of the carbon pricing policy and with the choice of income measure (annual vs. lifetime, household-level vs. per-capita with equivalence scales)?
data_description: The analysis combines three main data sources. Household consumption data come from the 2003 Consumer Expenditure Survey (CES) from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, providing annual household expenditures across roughly 109 consumption categories (food, shelter, electricity, natural gas, gasoline, transportation, healthcare, etc.) by income quintile, along with after-tax income, household size, and number of income earners. Households with annual income below $7,500 are excluded. Emissions intensities come from the Carnegie Mellon University Economic Input-Output Life Cycle Assessment (EIO-LCA) model, based on the 1997 US Bureau of Economic Analysis input-output tables covering 491 industrial sectors, which yields tons of CO2 and CO2-equivalent greenhouse gases emitted per dollar of sectoral output. Direct emissions from gasoline combustion and natural gas use are added using EPA emissions factors. The unit of observation is the household (and per-capita equivalents), with a hypothetical carbon price of $15 per ton of CO2.
institutional_context: The study is motivated by active US policy debates over national greenhouse gas legislation under the Obama Administration, including proposals for a federal carbon tax and, more prominently, cap-and-trade programs such as the Waxman-Markey bill considered by Congress. Both instruments would, for the first time in the US, impose a price on each ton of CO2 emitted, with compliance costs ultimately passed through to consumers via higher prices for energy-intensive goods such as electricity, gasoline, natural gas, and food. Because energy expenditures constitute a larger share of budgets for lower-income households, policymakers and the public are particularly concerned about the equity consequences of pricing carbon. The institutional setting also includes existing federal taxes (payroll/FICA, income, excise) whose revenues and structures could potentially be modified through revenue recycling to offset adverse distributional outcomes from carbon pricing. Allowance prices around $15 per ton of CO2 are within the range estimated by the EPA for these proposals.
